question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of facial hair growth, acne, and irregular menses. Her friends have told her that her voice sounds lower than usual. Physical examination shows pustular acne and dark hair growth along the jawline. Serum studies show elevated testosterone levels and normal inhibin levels. An ultrasound of the pelvis shows a left-sided ovarian mass. Microscopic examination of the resected ovarian mass shows pale, testosterone-positive staining cells with cytoplasmic Reinke crystal inclusions. These abnormal cells are homologous to which of the following physiological cell type in females?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Elevated testosterone levels" -> "Facial hair growth, acne, irregular menses" -> "Lower voice pitch" -> "Dark hair growth along the jawline" -> "Pustular acne" -> "Ovarian mass on ultrasound" -> "Testosterone-positive staining cells with Reinke crystal inclusions" -> "Theca interna cells" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Elevated testosterone levels" -> "Facial hair growth, acne, irregular menses" -> "Lower voice pitch" -> "Dark hair growth along the jawline" -> "Pustular acne" -> "Ovarian mass on ultrasound" -> "Testosterone-positive staining cells with Reinke crystal inclusions" -> "Granulosa cells" -> 90%
enhanced_information: The abnormal cells with Reinke crystal inclusions found in the ovarian mass are homologous to Theca interna cells, not Granulosa cells as previously thought. This conclusion is supported by the presence of testosterone-positive staining cells. The elevated testosterone levels, facial hair growth, acne, irregular menses, lower voice pitch, dark hair growth along the jawline, and pustular acne are all consistent with this diagnosis.
analysis: The patient's presentation of hirsutism, acne, irregular menses, and the presence of an ovarian mass with testosterone-positive staining cells containing Reinke crystal inclusions point towards a diagnosis of an androgen-secreting tumor. The cells in question are homologous to Theca interna cells, which are responsible for androgen production in the ovary. This aligns with the clinical and histological findings in this case.
